Syed Istiaque Ahmed with Shafique Ahmed and Kazi Kamrul Alam, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners 
Mahmudul Islam, Attorney-General with Obaidul Hasan Shaheen, Assistant Attorney General, Bazlur Rahman Sana, Assistant Attorney General and Naima Haidar, Assistant Attorney General ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Shawn Apparels Ltd ------ Petitioner
vs
Commissioner of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
3. The respondent Nos. 1-3 are contesting the Rule by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition wherein they have denied the material allegations made in the writ petition and contended that the containers in question entered in Chittagong port in the month of October, 1997 while the Master LC of the petitioner was established long thereafter on 16-3-98 and on the basis of Master LC back to back LC was established by the petitioner on 31-3-98. The bills of lading originally submitted for these containers showed the consignee as to the order of Agrani Bank Tejgaon Industrial Area Branch which suggests that the LCs were opened by Agrani Bank, Tejgaon Industrial Area Branch for the said consignee but no such LCs were however produced for clearance of the consignments. It is further contended that at a later stage when the Customs Intelligence reported malpractice, an enquiry was made by the Deputy Commissioner of Customs wherein it was revealed that no letter of credit was opened by the Agrani Bank for the import of the goods in question. It is, thus, detected that the goods in question were brought into Bangladesh under fictitious non-existent LCs. It is further asserted that the 40 ft container arrived at Chittagong port on 1- 10-97 and 20 ft container arrived at Chittagong on 5-11-97 without the cover of any LC and effort was made to hoodwink the customs officials by making false statement in the Bills of Lading. The containers in question were brought into Bangladesh in blatant violation of the Import Policy Order and in view of the provisions of section 2(s) read with section 16 of the Customs Act, 1969 (hereinafter called the Act) the goods in question were smuggled goods liable to be confiscated under section 156(9) of the Act. It is further contended that the 40 ft container was brought to Bangladesh through the carrier, Advance Container Lines (pvt) Ltd and on 1-10-97 delivered IGM bearing Rotation No 964/97. In the said IGM the local shipping agent was shown as the importer of the said consignment. On 6-11-97 the local shipping agent filed an application for substitution of the name of the shipping agent by the name of Sathi Apparels as importer in the IGM and the Customs Authority without suspecting any foul play allowed the substitution Thereafter the shipping agent surreptitiously changed the name of importer from Sathi Apparels to Unipex Knit Ware Ltd in IGM and submitted it to Port Authority and thereafter the petitioner entered into the scene and an application was filed to change the name of importer in the IGM from Unipex Knit Ware Ltd to Shawn Apparels Ltd and concerned Customs officer allowed the substitution without inquiring how Unipex Knit Ware Ltd could come in the picture-in place of Sathi Apparels. 

 4. The 40 ft container was shipped on board the vessel of Continental Lines International on 1-10-97 which arrived at Chittagong port on 5-11-97. In IGM bearing rotation No. 979 of 1997 the importer of the container was shown as Unipex Knit Ware Ltd. and on the application of the local shipping agent the name of the importer was changed to Sathi Apparels in the IGM and the change was notified by letter dated 9-11-97 but again on the application of the shipping agent the name of the importer was changed to Shawn Apparels Ltd, that is, the petitioner in place of Sathi Apparels. In this case also the concerned Customs officer failed to enquire how Sathi Apparels is dropped. It is stated that at the stage the name of Sathi Apparels was incorporated in the IGM of the two containers and the said Sathi Apparels did not appear and did not file any document for release of the goods in question and the disappearance of the name of the Sathi Apparels from the IGM attracted the notice of some Customs Officials who on 6-5-98 made a note in the file for adjudication of the matter but the Commissioner of Customs without going deep into the matter incidentally treated it to be a valid import and treating the discrepancy to be a technical violation imposed a fine of Taka 10,000.00 only. This noting dated 10-5-98 in the file was not communicated to the petitioner but coming to know about it the petitioner to cover up the matter in hot haste paid the fine and tried to take delivery of the containers. But on the same day the Customs Intelligence made a report suspecting foul play and as a result delivery of the consignments was suspended and an enquiry was started. On enquiry made-by the Customs Intelligence arid Investigating Cell it was found that there was no such company in the name of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd but however a company under the name and style of Unipex Apparels Ltd was in existence at 21/5. Nurjahan Road and it denied to have opened any LC or obtained invoice for the goods of the containers in question and then it became clear that the containers were brought into Bangladesh in the name of fictitious and non-existent importers. The National Board or Revenue on being informed about the said incident passed an order for detention of the consignment by the letter dated 30-6-98 and thereafter an enquiry was made about the opening of LC by Agrani Bank and it became clear that the goods were brought under false name and under fictitious LCs and it was a clear attempt to smuggle the goods into Bangladesh and in that view of the matter the impugned letter was issued by the respondents stopping delivery of the goods and seizing the same under section 156(9) of the Customs Act. 

 7. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Attorney General appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-3, on the other hand, submits that it is clear from the materials on record that in the instant case the customs officials failed to discharge their duties in accordance with law and in passing the order for imposing fine of an amount of Taka 10,000.00 on the ground of technical violation of the Import policy order is absolutely illegal and without any legal basis inasmuch as it is apparent from the paragraph Nos. 6-8 of the note sheets of the relevant file that the correct legal position was brought to the notice of the respondent No. 1, but when the matter was placed before the Joint Commissioner of Customs the petitioner company filed an application for summary adjudication under section 180 of the Customs Act but without any adjudication made by the customs officials under section 180 of the Customs Act the respondents No. 1 under a mistaken view of law and fact termed the violation as a technical violation of the Import policy order and thus passed an order imposing a fine of Taka 10,000.00 only for their failure to submit the necessary Import permit. The learned Attorney- General further submits that it is clear from the documents annexed with the writ petition as well as the affidavit-in-opposition that an attempt was made by someone to import the goods in question evading taxes and it is clear from the materials on record that the goods in question were shipped by the supplier and arrived at Chittagong port in October, 1997 without any valid LCs for the said goods in question. The learned Attorney-General further submits that it is clear from the Papers annexed by the petitioner in their writ petition that the 40 ft container was imported by the shipping agent PIL (BD) Ltd and it is prohibited by law that no shipping agent can import any goods in Bangladesh. The learned Attorney-General further submits that from the documents annexed with the application as well as the Affidavit-in-opposition it is clear that for both the containers the name of Sathi Apparels were substituted in place of original consignees but subsequently the said Sathi Apparels name was dropped and the name of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd. was substituted without any material basis and the .petitioner at the time of opening of the LC knew that the goods were at Chittagong port in the Customs godown for a pretty long period and they must have opened the LC knowing fully well that those goods lying there are smuggled goods because they were not brought into Bangladesh under the coverage of any LC. The learned Attorney-General further submits that the Master LC was opened by the petitioner on 16-3-98 and they opened the back to back LC on 31-3-98 whereas the goods were already in Bangladesh in October, 1997 and in that view of the matter, they ought to have enquired about the situation of the goods lying in the Customs Godown and as to the title of the seller. He further submits that it thus appears that the petitioner knowing fully well that the goods in question were smuggled goods, opened the back to back LC on 31-3-98 to cover up the misdeed of the supplier. The learned Attorney-General further submits that there is no material basis whatsoever for invoking the doctrine of estoppel or the principle of agency inasmuch as the petitioner did not enter into the deal through the instrumentality of the Government officials The Government officials came in the scene only after the opening of the back to back LC when they applied for amendment of the IGM and that amendment has been made by the Customs Officials as they could not detect the illegality or irregularity with regard to the goods in question. The learned Attorney-General further submits that in this case the petitioner wants to prohibit the Government Officials from performing their legal duties and in that view of the matter as well the doctrine of estoppel has no manner of application because it is now well settled that there cannot be any estoppel against law and. in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported in AIR 1937, (PC) 114. The learned Attorney-General further submits that from the materials on, record it is clear that there has been illegality committed by someone in bringing the goods in Bangladesh without valid authority and thus it is attracted by the provisions of section 2(s) of the Customs Act and became smuggled goods within the meaning of that section as the goods were brought into Bangladesh with a view to evade the customs duty and in that view of the matter on the report of the Customs Intelligence and Investigating Cell the Board of Revenue rightly directed the customs officials to stop delivery of the goods and seized the same under section 168(1) of the Customs Act as the goods are liable to be confiscated under section 156(9) of the Customs Act. The learned Attorney-General further submits that there is not an iota of evidence on record or any materials to show that the customs authority had ever adjudicated the matter under section 180 of the Customs Act and there are no materials on record to show that the fine of Taka 10,000.00 was imposed on the petitioner under section 181 of the Customs Act in lieu of confiscation of the goods rather, it is clear from the concerned file that the respondent, No. 1 imposed the penalty of Taka 10,000.60 by way of fine for failure of the petitioner to submit the necessary Import permit. The learned Attorney-General further submits, that the instant Rule is not maintainable in view of the provisions of section 193 of the Customs Act inasmuch as a person is authorised to prefer an appeal against any decision or order passed by the customs officials and in that view of the matter the petitioner if aggrieved could prefer an appeal to the Appellate Commissioner under section 193 of the Customs Act and the provisions of' appeal as provided therein is  equally efficacious and speedy remedy because there is no question of deposit of any amount by way of customs duty and there is no legal bar imposed on the appellate Commissioner to pass any ad-interim order pending disposal of the appeal. The, learned Attorney- General further submits that in the instant case the shipper applied for an amendment of the IGM but it is prohibited by law because shipping Agents are not authorised by law to import goods inasmuch as they are not registered under the Importers and Exporters and Indentors (Registration) Order, 1989 and, as such, they were not permitted to open any LC. The learned Attorney-General further submits that the two consignments were by amendment shown to have been imported by Sathi Apparels but the name of the importers could not be changed to Shawn Apparels Ltd that is, in the petitioner's name without the written consent or No' Objection certificate from Sathi Apparels and in the instant case No Objection Certificate from the Sathi Apparels was produced before the authority and, as such, the change of the names of the importers were unauthorised, illegal and without jurisdiction. The learned Attorney General further submits that from Annexures "5" and "10" of the Affidavit-in-Opposition it is clear that the containers in question, that is the 40 ft container was imported by PIL (ED) Ltd and the 20 ft container, was imported by Unipex Knit Ware Ltd and it is revealed from record that PIL (BD) Ltd as Shipping Agent cannot import any goods from abroad and the' alleged importer for the 20 ft container namely Unipex were also found to be non-existent and these documents have not been denied by the petitioner and from these documents it is clear and apparent that the containers in question containing the goods were brought into Bangladesh without any valid authority and in the name of fictitious importers. The learned Attorney-General referring to Annexure "D-1" annexed to the writ petition and Annexures "1" and "2" of the Affidavit-in-Opposition submits that in the instant case there is a peculiar situation wherein two original bills of lading were submitted for the self-same goods by the shipper on the same date with same number which is practically impossible and this establishes beyond any shadow of doubt that there has been a foul play in importing the goods in question by the petitioner and the petitioner had sufficient knowledge at the time of opening the LC on 31-3- 98 mat the goods in question have been brought into Bangladesh through an illegal means. 

 9. From a perusal of the records it appears that after the opening of the LC the petitioner for the first time through their local agent applied to the Customs Authority for amendment of IGM and to insert their name in place of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd in respect of 40 ft container and vide Annexure "F" similarly the IGM in respect of 20 ft container was amended and their name was inserted in place of Unipex Ltd but from the papers annexed with the affidavit-in-opposition it appears that the 40 ft container was amended by PIL(BD) Ltd, a shipping agent in Bangladesh. Thereafter, the IGM was amended and the name of Sathi Apparels was inserted in place of PIL (BD) Ltd for which an application for amendment of the IGM was submitted by PIL (BD) Ltd on 6th November, 1997 to the Additional Commissioner of Customs, ICD Kamalapur and that application was allowed and the name of Sathi Enterprise was inserted in place of PIL (BD) Ltd and that order was communicated to PIL vide Annexure "7" dated 11-9-97. From Annexure "8" it appears that subsequently another application was filed before the Deputy Commissioner of Customs on 27th of April, 1998 for amendment of IGM wherein it has been stated that due to mistake supplier's name was wrongly inserted as Unipex Knit Ware Ltd which should be, in fact Shawan Apparels Ltd ie the petitioner. In this connection it has been asserted by the respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition that the shipping agent surreptitiously inserted the name of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd in the amended IGM in place of Sathi Enterprise and thereafter the said application on 27th of April, 1998 for amendment of the IGM and accordingly, vide Annexure "9' the Customs-Authority amended the IGM and inserted the name of the petitioner in place of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd but there is nothing on record to show that this 40 ft container was ever either imported by Unipex Knit Ware Ltd or their name Was inserted at a subsequent stage by amending the IGM in question. It thus appears that the contention raised by the respondents that the shipping agent surreptitiously beyond the knowledge of the customs authority has inserted the name of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd in place of Sathi Enterprise is well founded. It thus also appears that in amending the IGM the customs officials are at least guilty of latches and negligence as they did not at all take due care to enquire into the vital aspect of the case as to how the name of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd was inserted in the amended IGM. It shows that to ,cover up the illegal importation of the goods in question the petitioner in connivance with the shipping agent and customs officials concerned have done one after another mischief by amending the 10M without verifying the necessary documents. In this connection it may be mentioned that the 20 ft container was allegedly imported by Unipex Knit Ware Ltd and we have already noticed that for the importation of the said container as well there was no valid LC opened by the alleged importer Unipex Knit Ware Ltd and the Tejgaon Industrial Branch of the Agrani Bank have stoutly denied to have opened any such LC for importing the said container. From Annexure "11" to the Affidavit-in-opposition it appears that an application was filed by Gold view Shipping Ltd as agent to amend the IGM for the 20 ft container and to insert the name of Sathi Apparels of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd and this was allowed and the name of the Sathi Apparels was substituted in place of Unipex Knit Wire Ltd which is evidenced by Annexure "12" to the Affidavit-in-Opposition but greatly to our surprise it appears that the self-same shipping agent on 8-11-97 submitted another application for amendment of the concerned IGM wherein it has been stated that the name of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd has been wrongly included in the IGM which should be Shawn Apparels Ltd, that is the petitioner company and pursuant to this application vide Annexure '14' to the Affidavit-in-Opposition the IGM was amended and the name of the petitioner was substituted for Unipex Knit Ware Ltd whereas it appears from Annexures "11" and "12" that in place of original consignee the name of Sathi Apparels was substituted and suppressing this fact the subsequent application was filed by the Gold view Shipping Ltd as agent to the customs authority' for substitution of the name of the petitioner in place of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd. On top of that it has been found on investigation by the Intelligence and Investigating Cell of Customs that there is no existence of any such company under the name and style of Unipex Knit Ware Ltd in the given address. However, there is another company in the name .and style of Unipex Apparels Ltd at a different address and the Managing Director of the said company also expressed his ignorance as to the opening of any LC for the said 20 ft container. These facts go to show beyond any doubt that both the containers were brought Into Bangladesh in an illegal way by flouting the provisions' of the Customs Act and with the ill motive of evading customs duty. The petitioner could not deny or dispute the documents annexed with the Affidavit- in-Opposition. It, thus appears to us that the goods in question entered into Bangladesh on 1-10-97 and 5-11-97 illegally and without any valid authority, that the goods in question were brought into Bangladesh illegally and with the ill motive of evading the Customs duty is evident from the fact that even after the unloading of the said goods and storing the same in the 'Customs godown none approached the Customs authority within the span of seven months to clear the goods in question and in the meantime the petitioner appeared in the scene and opened the back to back LC on 31-3-98 long after the arrival of the goods in question and with ante dated Bill of Lading tried to get the goods cleared. But it appears from the concerned file that the Deputy Collector of Customs initially correctly detected that the importers have failed to clear the goods within seven months from the date of landing of the same and there has been violation of Article 16(6) (j) of the Import Policy Order and the original Bill of Lading was not submitted even after the expiry of six months and hence note was initiated for a decision in the matter and the same was placed before the Joint Commissioner of Customs. From paragraph No.9 of the note sheet it appears that the Joint Commissioner also agreed with the. Deputy Collector that there has been a violation of the provision of Import Policy Order and asked the petitioner to file Import permit. In paragraph No. 10 of the note sheet it appears that the petitioner expressed their inability to file the necessary Import permit but at the same time filed an application for summary adjudication under the provisions of section 180 of the Customs Act. From subsequent paragraph Nos. 11, 12 and 13 it appears that there has been no adjudication by the customs officials under section 180 of the Customs Act rather after assessing the customs duty on the goods in question the Collector of Customs passed an order imposing a fine of Taka 10,000.00 on the petitioner for technical violation of the Import Policy Order From a careful consideration of the contents of the said paragraphs it clearly emerges that although the petitioner filed an application under section 180 of the Customs Act admitting his fault and prayed for summary adjudication but no such adjudication whatsoever was done by the customs' authority rather it appears that the Commissioner of Customs is of opinion that there has been a technical violation of Article 16(6)(j) of the Import Policy Order and observed that since it is a case of technical violation it should be leniently dealt with and imposed the aforesaid fine. It is asserted by the respondents that the said order was never communicated by the Customs Officials to the petitioner but it appears to us that the petitioner had access to the concerned file of the customs authority and somehow came to know that such an order had been passed and managed to pay the fine vide Annexure 'H' to the application on 12-5-98. The customs officials also endorsed Annexure 'R' for payment of the fine. It is asserted by the petitioner most emphatically both in the writ petition as well as in the Affidavit-in-Reply there had been an adjudication by the customs authority under section 180 of the Customs Act in respect of the goods and to substantiate that contention they have only Annexure 'H' and nothing else. We have perused the concerned file to which we have already referred to and it appears to us that the fine in question was imposed for violating Article 16(6)(j) of the Import Policy Order and not on adjudication under section 180 of the Act and the fine was not imposed under section 181 of the Act. Section 181 of the Customs Act runs as follows: 

 12. From the aforesaid facts and circumstances it is clear that the customs officials holding the highest posts are in the habit of discharging their duties in a very negligent way to the detriment of the interest of the country. That the customs officials were discharging their duties in this matter with utter disregard, to the provisions of law is demonstrated by the fact that it was initially brought to the notice of the Joint Commissioner of Customs as well as to the Commissioner of Customs by the Deputy Commissioner of Customs that even after the expiry of six months the consignee could not produce original Bill of Lading and, as such, they ought to have confiscated the goods outright and sold the same through auction but for reasons best known to them they sat over the matter for obvious reasons which demonstrates their ill motive and nothing else.
